activity_context.topic_title: Asymptotes of Hyperbolas Centered at a General Point

feedback.problem: Calculate the asymptotes of the hyperbola $4{x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}+16x-20=0.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in standard form, we need to group the $x$ terms and complete the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}+16x-20 & =0 \\ (4{x}^{2}+16x)-9{y}^{2}-20 & =0 \\ 4[{x}^{2}+4x]-9{y}^{2}-20 & =0 \\ 4[(x+2)^{2}-4]-9{y}^{2}-20 & =0 \\ 4(x+2)^{2}-16-9{y}^{2}-20 & =0 \\ 4(x+2)^{2}-9{y}^{2} & =20+16 \\ 4(x+2)^{2}-9{y}^{2} & =36 \\ \frac{4(x+2)^{2}}{36}-\frac{9{y}^{2}}{36} & =\frac{36}{36} \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

The asymptotes of a horizontal hyperbola

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by 

$$
y-k=\pm \frac{b}{a}(x-h).
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
h=-2,\,k=0,\,a=\sqrt{9}=3,\,b=\sqrt{4}=2.
$$

Therefore, the asymptotes of the hyperbola are

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \frac{2}{3}(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$
